target.title: test(gateway): lock config mutation allowlist contract
target.body:
# PR: test(gateway): lock config mutation allowlist contract

**Branch:** `codex/gateway-config-allowlist-contract`  
**Commit:** `8424fcad05`  
**Compare:** https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/compare/main...hugenshen:codex/gateway-config-allowlist-contract?expand=1

---

## What Problem This Solves

The `gateway` built-in tool is a **persistent control-plane write surface**: agent-driven `config.apply` / `config.patch` can change live gateway config without operator CLI involvement. Per `SECURITY.md` and [Control plane tools risk](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security#control-plane-tools-risk), **the model/agent is not a trusted principal** — the runtime must fail closed and only permit a narrow, hand-maintained allowlist.

That allowlist lives in `src/agents/tools/gateway-tool.ts:54` as `ALLOWED_GATEWAY_CONFIG_PATHS`. Today it is a **mutable string array with no contract lock**:

| Existing coverage                                            | What it proves                                                                   | Gap                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `gateway-tool-guard-coverage.test.ts` (~43 behavioral cases) | Many real patches are allowed/blocked (auth, plugins, sandbox, hooks, MCP, etc.) | Does **not** fail when someone adds/removes/reorders allowlist patterns        |
| `gateway-tool.test.ts`                                       | Tool schema exposes `replacePaths`; description mentions it                      | Does **not** exercise guard semantics with `replacePaths`                      |
| `src/gateway/server.config-patch.test.ts`                    | Gateway RPC rejects destructive array shrinks without `replacePaths`             | Tests **server merge policy**, not the gateway-tool path allowlist after merge |

**Risk without this PR:** a maintainer can widen the agent-tunable surface (e.g. add `plugins.allow`, `gateway.auth.token`, `tools.exec.host`) and existing guard tests may still pass if nobody adds a new behavioral case. The allowlist drift stays invisible until review catches it manually.

---

## Why This Change Was Made

Add a **focused contract test** that complements (not replaces) `gateway-tool-guard-coverage.test.ts`:

1. **Snapshot lock** — exact sorted contents of `ALLOWED_GATEWAY_CONFIG_PATHS` (18 patterns today)
2. **Compact forbidden-path table** — representative high-impact paths that must stay blocked
3. **`replacePaths` guard boundary** — wholesale `agents.list` replacement must still respect the allowlist

Minimal prod change: export the allowlist for tests only (`ALLOWED_GATEWAY_CONFIG_PATHS_FOR_TEST`). No runtime behavior change.

---

## Security / Trust Boundary Context

`assertGatewayConfigMutationAllowed` (`gateway-tool.ts:379`) is the model → operator trust gate. It runs **before** the gateway RPC and applies two independent checks:

```
config.patch / config.apply raw
        │
        ▼
 applyMergePatch (mergeObjectArraysById + optional replacePaths)
        │
        ▼
 collectChangedConfigPaths(current, next)
        │
        ├─► Gate 1: every changed path must match ALLOWED_GATEWAY_CONFIG_PATHS
        │         (prefix match; `*` = one segment wildcard)
        │
        └─► Gate 2: newly enabled dangerous flags blocked
                  (same enumeration as `openclaw security audit`)
```

**Gate 1** is what this PR locks. **Gate 2** (dangerous flags) remains covered by existing guard-coverage cases (e.g. `browser.ssrfPolicy`, `sandbox.docker.dangerouslyAllowContainerNamespaceJoin`).

Public docs already describe the intended contract:

> Agent-driven `gateway config.apply` and `gateway config.patch` edits are fail-closed by default: only a narrow set of low-risk runtime tuning, mention-gating, and visible-reply paths are agent-tunable. Global model defaults and prompt overlays stay operator-controlled.

— [Control plane tools risk](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security#control-plane-tools-risk)

---

## Locked Allowlist (18 patterns)

| Category                         | Patterns                                                                                                         | Rationale                                                  |
| -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Agent runtime tuning (defaults)  | `agents.defaults.thinkingDefault`, `.subagents.thinking`, `.reasoningDefault`, `.fastModeDefault`                | Low-risk model behavior knobs                              |
| Agent runtime tuning (per-agent) | `agents.list[].id`, `.model`, `.thinkingDefault`, `.subagents.thinking`, `.reasoningDefault`, `.fastModeDefault` | Scoped per-agent tuning only                               |
| Mention gating (depth 1–5)       | `channels.*.requireMention` … `channels.*.*.*.*.*.requireMention`                                                | Must cover deepest adapter path (Telegram topic overrides) |
| Visible reply UX                 | `messages.visibleReplies`, `messages.groupChat.visibleReplies`, `messages.groupChat.unmentionedInbound`          | Bounded delivery UX, not secrets/privilege                 |

**Explicitly NOT on the allowlist** (operator-only): `gateway.auth.*`, `plugins.allow`, `plugins.load.paths`, `tools.exec.*`, `hooks.*`, global `agents.defaults.model`, prompt overlays, sandbox overrides, MCP servers, etc. — already blocked in guard-coverage; this PR adds contract-level regression for three canonical forbidden paths.

---

## New Test Coverage

**File:** `src/agents/tools/gateway-tool-allowlist.contract.test.ts`

| Test                                                                                 | Asserts                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `locks the exact allowed path patterns`                                              | Sorted snapshot of all 18 patterns; any add/remove/reorder fails CI |
| `blocks protected path mutations: gateway.auth.token`                                | Auth secret rewrite blocked                                         |
| `blocks protected path mutations: plugins.allow`                                     | Plugin trust boundary blocked                                       |
| `blocks protected path mutations: tools.exec.host`                                   | Exec routing escalation blocked                                     |
| `allows agents.list wholesale replace via replacePaths when edits stay allowlisted`  | `replacePaths: ["agents.list"]` + model-only change passes          |
| `blocks agents.list wholesale replace via replacePaths when protected fields change` | `replacePaths: ["agents.list"]` + `sandbox` change still blocked    |

### `replacePaths` semantics covered here

- **Without** `replacePaths`: id-keyed merge (default) — already heavily tested in guard-coverage
- **With** `replacePaths: ["agents.list"]`: whole-array replacement is simulated at the **gateway-tool guard** layer
- **Server-side** destructive-array rules (`server.config-patch.test.ts`) are orthogonal; this PR ensures the tool guard still fail-closes protected nested fields even when the caller opts into array replacement

---

## User Impact

- **Runtime:** none
- **Operators:** none
- **Maintainers:** intentional allowlist changes require updating both:
  1. `ALLOWED_GATEWAY_CONFIG_PATHS` in `gateway-tool.ts`
  2. `LOCKED_ALLOWLIST` in `gateway-tool-allowlist.contract.test.ts`

  That is intentional — widening the agent-tunable surface should be a deliberate, reviewed act.

---

## Evidence

### Local proof

```sh
pnpm test src/agents/tools/gateway-tool-allowlist.contract.test.ts
node --import tsx scripts/proof-gateway-allowlist-contract.mjs
```

```
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  6 passed (6)
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Agent-driven `gateway config.patch` must fail closed on protected paths and accept only allowlisted mutations.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS (Darwin), Node.js v22.22.0.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  1. `node --import tsx scripts/proof-gateway-allowlist-contract.mjs`
  2. `pnpm test src/agents/tools/gateway-tool-allowlist.contract.test.ts`
- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-gateway-allowlist-contract.mjs
=== gateway config.patch guard (production assertGatewayConfigMutationAllowed) ===
  ok: allowlisted agents.defaults.thinkingDefault patch accepted
allowlisted patch: agents.defaults.thinkingDefault off -> on
  ok: protected gateway.auth.token patch rejected
protected patch error: Error: gateway config.patch cannot change protected config paths: gateway.auth.token
  ok: replacePaths agents.list model-only change accepted

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Allowlisted thinking-default patch passes; `gateway.auth.token` rewrite is rejected with the production guard error; `replacePaths: ["agents.list"]` still respects the allowlist for model-only edits.
- **What was not tested:** Live gateway RPC round-trip; proof exercises the same production guard used by the gateway tool before RPC.

### Diff size

```
src/agents/tools/gateway-tool.ts                        | +3   (test-only export)
src/agents/tools/gateway-tool-allowlist.contract.test.ts | +103 (contract tests)
```

### Evidence map

| Surface                       | Entry point                              | Owner                       | Caller                                         | Sibling                           | Tests                                               |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Gateway config mutation guard | `assertGatewayConfigMutationAllowed`     | `gateway-tool.ts`           | `createGatewayTool` config.apply/patch actions | Gateway server `config.patch` RPC | **This PR** + `gateway-tool-guard-coverage.test.ts` |
| Dangerous flag gate           | `collectEnabledInsecureOrDangerousFlags` | `dangerous-config-flags.ts` | same guard                                     | `openclaw security audit`         | guard-coverage (unchanged)                          |
| Array merge policy            | `applyMergePatch` + `replacePaths`       | `merge-patch.ts`            | gateway-tool + gateway RPC                     | `server.config-patch.test.ts`     | **This PR** (tool guard slice) + server tests       |

---

## Out of Scope / Follow-ups

This PR does **not**:

- Extract `ALLOWED_GATEWAY_CONFIG_PATHS` into schema-derived metadata (separate maintenance PR)
- Add security-audit reachability findings for open channels + `gateway` tool exposure (separate audit PR)
- Duplicate all 43 guard-coverage behavioral cases in the contract file

Suggested follow-up if allowlist keeps growing: generate `LOCKED_ALLOWLIST` from a single exported constant or schema artifact to avoid dual-edit friction.

---

## Checklist

- [x] No runtime behavior change
- [x] Test-only export marked `@internal`
- [x] Fail-closed contract: widening allowlist requires explicit test update
- [x] `replacePaths` boundary covered at gateway-tool guard layer
- [ ] CI (pending upstream run after PR open)

---

## Create PR

```sh
gh pr create \
  --title "test(gateway): lock config mutation allowlist contract" \
  --body-file pr-gateway-allowlist-contract-body.md
```

Or open: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/compare/main...hugenshen:codex/gateway-config-allowlist-contract?expand=1

target.title: fix(discord): preserve content-type and skip optimization for animated/WebP images
target.body:
## Summary

- **Problem:** Discord media uploads were sending files without a MIME content-type, causing some clients/bots to misidentify the file format. Additionally, WebP images were being converted to JPEG (losing quality) and animated images (GIF, WebP, APNG) were being converted/optimized, destroying animation frames.
- **Why it matters:** Users sending WebP images or animated GIFs/APNGs via Discord and the web provider received degraded or broken output — silent data-loss bugs.
- **What changed:** `toDiscordFileBlob` now accepts and forwards a `contentType` to the `Blob` constructor; `loadWebMediaInternal` skips image optimization for GIF, WebP, and any animated image (detected via sharp's `pages` metadata); a new `isAnimatedImage` helper was added to `image-ops.ts`.
- **What did NOT change:** Non-animated JPEG/PNG optimization paths are unchanged; no other channels are affected.

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [x] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Closes #41256
- Related #

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- WebP images sent via Discord or the web provider are no longer silently converted to JPEG.
- Animated GIFs and animated WebP/APNG files are no longer passed through the image optimizer (which would strip frames).
- Discord uploads now include the correct MIME type in the `Blob`, so recipients see the right file format.
- Error messages for oversized GIF/WebP/animated images now include a more specific label (`GIF`, `WebP`, `Animated image`) instead of the generic `Media`.

## Security Impact (required)

target.title: fix(browser): bound response text decoding
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Browser plugin's `responsebody` action used Playwright `Response.text()`. Playwright first obtains the complete response `Buffer` and then decodes the entire body into a JavaScript string, even though OpenClaw returns at most `maxChars`. Large responses therefore caused an avoidable second full-body allocation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The rewritten change keeps one passive Playwright response path and preserves the existing response prefix. It calls `Response.body()` once, decodes only `maxChars * 4` bytes (the maximum UTF-8 input needed for `maxChars` characters), then applies the existing character bound.

This is the strongest safe fix available through Playwright 1.60.0's public API: [`Response.body()` returns the complete Buffer and `Response.text()` calls it before decoding](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/v1.60.0/packages/playwright-core/src/client/network.ts#L727-L733). OpenClaw can avoid the second large string allocation, but cannot prevent Playwright's initial body buffering without an upstream streaming API.

The earlier content-length omission and CLI-message paths were removed. Known-large and chunked responses keep the same user-visible prefix instead of returning an empty body, and page delivery remains untouched.

## User Impact

- `responsebody` still returns the requested response prefix and `truncated: true` for oversized bodies.
- The page still receives the complete original response.
- OpenClaw no longer creates a full decoded string merely to return a bounded prefix.
- No config, auth, protocol, or browser-support changes.

## Evidence

Exact PR head: `781780e54dd183fa7d23ad1ceb141c197a80a52f`

- [Hosted CI run `28832020533`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/28832020533): all selected checks passed; CodeQL completed neutral.
- Sanitized direct-AWS run `run_787bc7b5b70a` on fresh public-network lease `cbx_b5acd2f3429c` (`coral-prawn`, `c7a.8xlarge`): focused regression suite passed 12/12.
- The same exact-head run started a real Gateway and managed Chrome, returned `xxxxxxxxxx` with `truncated: true` from a 500,000-character response, and confirmed the page retained all 500,000 characters.
- The same run invoked an `openai/gpt-5.4` agent through the Gateway; the agent used the Browser tool against the live page and returned `RESPONSE_AGENT_OK`.
- Final-head autoreview against current `origin/main`: no actionable findings.

The live scenario serves a 500,000-character response, asserts that `responsebody --max-chars 10` returns `xxxxxxxxxx` with `truncated: true`, verifies the page received all 500,000 characters, then asks an `openai/gpt-5.4` agent through a real Gateway to open a second page with the Browser tool and return its marker.

## Scope and Limitations

This bounds OpenClaw's text decoding, not Playwright's initial response Buffer. No claim is made that the public Playwright API provides a fully streaming or constant-memory body read.

target.title: fix(ios): persist voice notes through offline delivery
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The iOS voice-note composer added in #100946 could lose its only attachment bytes after staging, an ambiguous send, app recreation, or an offline send. It could also retarget an in-progress recording when the selected chat changed, and microphone ownership could overlap with Talk or push-to-talk.

Relates to #100709 and follows up #100946.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Persist voice-note bytes in the existing per-gateway SQLite chat outbox before modern-Gateway delivery, with bounded per-command and total attachment budgets.
- Pin the captured session, agent, gateway, and routing contract from recording through staging and canonical confirmation.
- Keep recipient presentation pinned to that captured route, including after canonical history replaces the queued bubble.
- Make staging a one-shot recorder state so SwiftUI updates cannot consume the same file twice.
- Queue recordings while offline, preserve ambiguous delivery for reconciliation, and delete durable bytes only after canonical history confirms the user turn.
- Preserve the established live attachment path for healthy older Gateways that do not support safe replay leases.
- Serialize voice-note, Talk, push-to-talk, interruption, and background microphone ownership.

## User Impact

Voice notes can be recorded and sent while offline, survive reconnects and app recreation, and deliver once without changing chats or disappearing after an uncertain network result. Healthy older Gateways continue to send attachments live; durable offline replay requires a Gateway with the routing-contract capability.

## Evidence

- `swift test --filter 'VoiceNoteRecorderTests|ChatViewModelAttachmentTests|ChatTranscriptCacheStoreTests'`: 66 tests passed.
- `xcodebuild -project OpenClaw.xcodeproj -scheme OpenClaw -configuration Debug -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,id=F8D0EA37-7040-4FA7-8CFA-BA8841C68E1A' -derivedDataPath build/DerivedData test -only-testing:OpenClawTests/NodeAppModelInvokeTests`: 114 tests passed; signed simulator app, Watch app, widget, share extension, and shared packages built successfully.

target.title: feat(gateway): add allowedOriginPatterns for constrained loopback port wildcards
target.body:
Closes #98383

## What Problem This Solves

Remote WebView-hosted node clients (e.g. phone companion apps using Even Hub or similar frameworks) connect to the Gateway WebSocket with dynamically-assigned local origins like `http://127.0.0.1:<random-port>`. The current `gateway.controlUi.allowedOrigins` only supports exact origins or the global `["*"]` wildcard, forcing users to choose between two inadequate options:

- **Per-port allowlisting**: requires updating the config on every app restart, impractical for end users
- **`["*"]` wildcard**: disables browser origin checks entirely, a significant security regression

## Why This Change Was Made

Added `gateway.controlUi.allowedOriginPatterns` — a constrained pattern list that accepts only `scheme://loopback-host:*` patterns. The implementation touches three layers with clearly separated responsibilities:

**1. Zod schema (config load time — fail-close)**

Each pattern must pass six checks: valid format (`scheme://host:*`), explicit protocol (`http:` or `https:`), port-level `*` wildcard only, no host wildcards, and hostname in the loopback literal set (`127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, `[::1]`). Illegal patterns prevent service startup — no silent downgrades.

**2. Runtime matching (`checkBrowserOrigin`)**

A new `origin-pattern` matching branch is inserted between the existing allowlist check and the local-client fallback. This preserves exact-match priority (`allowedOrigins` wins over patterns) and all existing fallback paths (`host-header-fallback`, `private-same-origin`, `local-loopback`) remain untouched. The runtime also includes a redundant `isLoopbackHost` guard as defense-in-depth against non-loopback patterns that bypassed schema validation.

**3. Startup config validation**

- `server-runtime-config.ts`: the non-loopback bind check now accepts `allowedOriginPatterns` as valid origin configuration — users deploying on a public bind with only patterns configured will not be blocked
- `gateway-control-ui-origins.ts`: `hasConfiguredControlUiAllowedOrigins` recognizes patterns so the auto-seed logic does not overwrite explicit user configuration

**4. Codex review follow-up**

- `schema.help.ts`: aligned `allowedOriginPatterns` help text style with `allowedOrigins`, added "Patterns are evaluated alongside allowedOrigins; either match is sufficient for WebSocket access" to clarify the union relationship
- `origin-check.test.ts`: added two HTTP trusted-proxy path tests confirming `allowedOriginPatterns` is correctly propagated through `resolveHttpBrowserOriginPolicy` → `authorizeTrustedProxyBrowserOrigin` → `checkBrowserOrigin`
- `audit-gateway-config.ts`: updated security audit to recognize `allowedOriginPatterns` as valid origin configuration, suppressing false `allowed_origins_required` findings
- `zod-schema.ts`: added `.describe()` metadata for `allowedOriginPatterns`
- `schema.help.ts`: updated `allowedOrigins` help text to reference `allowedOriginPatterns` as a safer alternative for dynamic loopback port clients
- `docs/gateway/configuration-reference.md` and `docs/gateway/troubleshooting.md`: added `allowedOriginPatterns` to public docs and origin-error remediation guidance
- `docs/gateway/security/index.md`: added `allowedOriginPatterns` to Gateway security notes
- `docs/gateway/trusted-proxy-auth.md`: updated trusted-proxy guidance (4 references) to include `allowedOriginPatterns`
- `docs/gateway/security/audit-checks.md`: updated audit-check table description and config column
- `legacy-config-migrations.runtime.gateway.ts`: passed `allowedOriginPatterns` through doctor migration so `openclaw doctor --fix` does not seed exact origins over a patterns-only config
- `ui/src/i18n/locales/en.ts`: added Control UI origin-error guidance referencing `allowedOriginPatterns` for dynamic loopback port scenarios

**Design constraints preserved across the stack:**

- No regular expressions beyond the fixed format parser — no ReDoS surface
- No host wildcards, no protocol wildcards, no implicit IP equivalence (`localhost` ≠ `127.0.0.1`)
- No DNS queries — loopback detection is pure string literal matching
- Hostname normalization between `parseOrigin` and `parseOriginPattern` is consistent: trailing-dot stripping applied in both directions
- Non-goals: client/role scoping, exact-port matching, DNS-resolution-based detection, pre-parsed pattern caching (current per-call cost is ~500ns, negligible relative to WebSocket handshake)

## User Impact

Users hosting Gateway on a public (non-loopback) address can now configure:

```json
{
  "gateway": {
    "controlUi": {
      "allowedOriginPatterns": ["http://127.0.0.1:*"]
    }
  }
}
```

This allows WebSocket connections from any remote WebView running on `http://127.0.0.1:<any-port>` without resorting to `["*"]`. The full loopback family is supported (`127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, `[::1]`, both `http:` and `https:` protocols).

**No existing behavior is changed** — all of the following continue to work identically:

- `allowedOrigins` exact matches (higher priority than patterns)
- `allowedOrigins: ["*"]` global wildcard (unchanged)
- `isLocalClient` loopback fallback (unchanged)
- `host-header-fallback` (unchanged)
- `private-same-origin` for LAN/tailscale hosts (unchanged)
- Non-loopback deployments with explicit `allowedOrigins` (unchanged)

Users currently on `["*"]` for WebView support can migrate to `["http://127.0.0.1:*"]` and regain origin-check protection while maintaining the same operational behavior.

**Compatibility note:** `allowedOriginPatterns` is an optional new field that
defaults to an empty array. Existing configurations are fully backward-compatible;
no data migration or manual upgrade is required for existing deployments. The
Zod schema rejects illegal patterns at load time (fail-close), so once a valid
config is accepted, it will remain valid across future versions.

## Evidence

**Runtime verification** (`npx tsx` against real source, no mocks, no test framework):

```
30/30 tests passed

─── A: Zod Schema allowedOriginPatterns (11/11) ───
  ✅ A1: http://127.0.0.1:* accepted
  ✅ A2: http://localhost:* accepted
  ✅ A3: http://[::1]:* accepted
  ✅ A4: https://127.0.0.1:* accepted
  ✅ A5: non-loopback hostname rejected
  ✅ A6: exact port without * rejected
  ✅ A7: host wildcard http://*:* rejected
  ✅ A8: bare * rejected
  ✅ A9: ftp protocol rejected
  ✅ A10: empty patterns array accepted (no regression)
  ✅ A11: allowedOrigins + allowedOriginPatterns coexist

─── B: checkBrowserOrigin runtime matching (15/15) ───
  ✅ B1: http://127.0.0.1:40313 matches pattern [CORE ISSUE SCENARIO]
  ✅ B2: http://localhost:5173 matches http://localhost:*
  ✅ B3: http://[::1]:8080 matches http://[::1]:*
  ✅ B4: https://127.0.0.1:9000 matches https://127.0.0.1:*
  ✅ B5: http://127.0.0.1 (no explicit port) matches pattern
  ✅ B6: non-loopback origin blocked
  ✅ B7: localhost != 127.0.0.1 (no implicit equivalence)
  ✅ B8: protocol mismatch rejected
  ✅ B9: allowedOrigins exact match takes priority over patterns
  ✅ B10: existing * wildcard still works (no regression)
  ✅ B11: isLocalClient loopback fallback unchanged (no regression)
  ✅ B12: empty patterns does not create bypass
  ✅ B13: trailing dot normalization works (localhost. matches localhost)
  ✅ B14: first matching pattern in array wins
  ✅ B15: * in allowedOrigins + empty patterns still works

─── C: CSRF startup guard (4/4) ───
  ✅ C1: allowedOriginPatterns counts as configured origins
  ✅ C2: both empty → not configured (CSRF guard active)
  ✅ C3: allowedOrigins with values still works
  ✅ C4: host-header fallback still works
```

**Regression test suites** (vitest, all passing):

| Test suite | Result |
|-----------|--------|
| `src/gateway/origin-check.test.ts` | 136/136 passed |
| `src/gateway/server-runtime-config.test.ts` | 58/58 passed |
| `src/gateway/server.auth.browser-hardening.test.ts` | 28/28 passed |
| `src/security/audit-gateway-exposure.test.ts` | 16/16 passed |
| **Total** | **238/238 passed** |

<details>
<summary>Real Gateway/WebSocket end-to-end verification</summary>

Test config openclaw.json
{
  "gateway": {
    "mode": "local",
    "bind": "lan",
    "port": 18789,
    "controlUi": {
      "enabled": true,
      "allowedOrigins": [],
      "allowedOriginPatterns": [
        "http://127.0.0.1:*",
        "http://localhost:*"
      ],
      "dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback": false
    }
  }
}

target.title: fix(auto-reply): defer foreground fence creation to delivery time (lazy fence)
target.body:
## Summary

Defer `beginForegroundReplyFence` from inbound dispatch entry time to first actual delivery attempt. This prevents same-session concurrent messages from cancelling or interleaving each other.

## Behavior addressed

When message B arrives in the same session while message A is still generating its reply, the eager fence creation at inbound time causes B to immediately bump the generation counter. A's `shouldCancelForegroundReplyDelivery` check then finds a newer `visibleDeliveryGeneration` and cancels A's remaining delivery (data loss).

Even with a guard that prevents cancellation of active generations (PR #93845), the delivery order becomes interleaved: A first half → B complete → A remaining half.

## Root cause

`beginForegroundReplyFence(finalized)` is called at line 566 of `dispatchInboundMessageWithBufferedDispatcher`, before the agent even starts processing. This creates a new generation for every inbound message immediately, causing older generations to be seen as stale.

## Fix

Defer fence creation using a lazy getter:

```typescript
let foregroundReplyFence: ForegroundReplyFenceSnapshot | undefined;
const getForegroundReplyFence = () => {
  foregroundReplyFence ??= beginForegroundReplyFence(finalized);
  return foregroundReplyFence;
};
```

The fence is now created only when `beforeDeliver` or `deliver` is first called. If message A has not started delivering when B arrives, B's fence creation does not pre-empt A — both messages complete without cancellation or interleaving.

## Key changes

- `dispatch.ts`: Introduce lazy getter, make `beforeDeliver` always defined, use lazy fence in `deliver`, guard `onSettled` path
- `dispatch.freshness.test.ts`: Update expectations for lazy fence behavior, add two new scenarios (no-delivery fence avoidance, concurrent pending dispatch)

## Verification

Before fix — older message cancelled when newer message delivers first:
```
olderResult: { queuedFinal: false, counts: { tool: 0, block: 0, final: 0 } }
channel deliveries: [B final only]  ← A's reply lost
```

After fix — both messages complete, both delivered:
```
olderResult: { queuedFinal: true, counts: { tool: 0, block: 0, final: 1 } }
channel deliveries: [B final, A final]  ← full delivery preserved
```

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Same-session concurrent foreground reply cancellation due to eager fence creation at inbound time.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node 24.13.0, upstream/main at f06539d8ba. Worktree at `/home/0668000615/10239986/github/openclaw-worktrees/fix-93858-defer-foreground-fence`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
cd openclaw-worktrees/fix-93858-defer-foreground-fence
node ./node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run \
  src/auto-reply/dispatch.freshness.test.ts \
  src/auto-reply/dispatch.test.ts
```

**Evidence after fix**: terminal output captured from the `node` command above:

```
 ✓ allows an older foreground final after a newer inbound event for the
   same session target when the older dispatch has not yet started delivering
 ✓ keeps fresh settled delivery active when no ordinary delivery creates
   a foreground fence
 ✓ keeps an older foreground final when a newer same-session dispatch is
   pending before visible delivery
 ✓ keeps an older foreground final when a newer inbound has no visible
   delivery while beforeDeliver is pending
 ✓ keeps an older foreground final fenced while a newer visible delivery
   is unresolved
 ✓ keeps an older foreground final when a newer visible delivery fails
 ✓ suppresses an older foreground final when a newer delivery partially
   sends before failing
 ✓ keeps an older foreground final when a newer adapter reports non-visible
 ✓ suppresses an older foreground final when a newer settled hook reports
   visible delivery
 ✓ still runs stale generic settled hooks after a newer visible reply
 ✓ suppresses an older fresh settled delivery after a newer visible reply
 ✓ runs the settled delivery hook when dispatch fails after queueing a reply
 ✓ keeps concurrent foreground finals isolated for different targets
   sharing a session

2 files passed (2), 32 scenarios verified, all succeeded.
```

The first scenario is the key behavioral change: previously the older dispatch was cancelled (`queuedFinal: false`). With lazy fence, the older dispatch that has not yet created its fence is allowed to complete (`queuedFinal: true`) — no data loss.

Additional dispatch lifecycle verification (19 scenarios) also passed successfully.

**Observed result after fix**: Lazy fence prevents concurrent same-session messages from cancelling each other when the older dispatch has not yet started delivering. This eliminates both data loss (truncation) and message interleaving (A half → B → A half). When the older dispatch has already started delivering (beforeDeliver already called), the existing cancellation behavior is preserved — newer visible delivery can still suppress stale in-flight deliveries.

**What was not tested**: Multi-message roundtrip through a real messaging channel (telegram/discord/whatsapp) requiring two inbound messages within a ~100ms window — impractical to reproduce deterministically without a custom channel harness. The fence mechanism is timing-sensitive; the verification above exercises the full dispatch pipeline including the real fence state machine, reply resolution, and delivery queue.

## References

- Fixes #93858
- Related: #93831, #91914
- Alternative approach: #93845 (active generation guard — complementary but insufficient alone)

target.title: fix(plugins): detect orphan diagnostics with explicit code marker (2-part fix)
target.body:
## Problem

When a plugin is removed but its path remains in `plugins.load.paths`,
discovery.ts emits "plugin path not found" diagnostics without `pluginId`.
These orphan diagnostics persist in SQLite `diagnostics_json` across
restarts, but `hasStalePersistedPluginDiagnostics()` fails to detect
them as stale. The stale persisted index then blocks Gateway startup
with config validation errors.

## Root Cause -- Two Bugs, Both Required

### Bug 1: Imprecise stale detection (`plugin-registry-snapshot.ts`)

The original `!pluginId` blanket rule would mark legitimate diagnostics
without pluginId (e.g. source-overlay warnings) as stale, causing
perpetual rediscovery on every startup.

### Bug 2: Zod schema strips `code` field (`installed-plugin-index-store.ts`)

`PluginDiagnosticSchema` was missing the optional `code` field. Zod default
strip mode silently drops unknown fields during `safeParseWithSchema`,
so even after Bug 1 was fixed, the `code: "orphan-source-path"` marker
was lost during the SQLite read-write round-trip.

## Fix (3 commits)

### `74b3e4d` -- Explicit code marker
- `discovery.ts`: tag orphan diagnostics with `code: "orphan-source-path"`
- `manifest-types.ts`: add `"orphan-source-path"` to `PluginDiagnosticCode`
- `plugin-registry-snapshot.ts`: check `diag.code === "orphan-source-path"`
instead of the blanket `!pluginId` rule
- `plugin-registry-snapshot.test.ts`: updated/added test cases

### `79ea25d` -- Zod schema round-trip fix
- `installed-plugin-index-store.ts`: add `code: z.string().optional()` to
`PluginDiagnosticSchema` so the `code` field survives read-write round-trip

### `5e71b53` -- Lint fix
- Remove unused test helper `expectDiagnosticsContainSource`

## Verification

- [x] Unit tests: 20/20 passed (`plugin-registry-snapshot.test.ts`)
- [x] No production impact, isolated environment cleaned up
- [x] Bishop review: approved

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Orphan diagnostics from removed plugins
block Gateway startup because `hasStalePersistedPluginDiagnostics()` fails
to detect them as stale, causing the persisted index to be used directly
for config validation (which fails because paths are missing).

- **Real environment tested**: Windows Server 2019 (Build 17763), Node.js
v24.16.0, isolated OpenClaw environment with 5-variable isolation
(`OPENCLAW_HOME`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`,
`OPENCLAW_DISABLE_BUNDLED_PLUGINS=1`, `HOME`) on port 18790.

- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
1. Generate orphan diagnostic by configuring a plugin path that does not exist
2. `loadInstalledPluginIndex()` generates diagnostic with
   `code: "orphan-source-path"`
3. `writePersistedInstalledPluginIndexSync()` persists to SQLite
4. `readPersistedInstalledPluginIndexSync()` reads back from SQLite
5. `loadPluginRegistrySnapshotWithMetadata()` gets snapshot
6. Verify snapshot `source` is `"derived"` (stale detected, re-derived index)

- **Evidence after fix**:

The `code` field survives the full SQLite write-read round-trip:

```
=== Phase 1: Generated diagnostic ===
{
  "level": "error",
  "message": "plugin path not found: C:\\Users\\...\\gone-plugin",
  "source": "C:\\Users\\...\\gone-plugin",
  "code": "orphan-source-path"
}

=== Phase 2: After write-read round-trip (fix applied) ===
{
  "level": "error",
  "message": "plugin path not found: C:\\Users\\...\\gone-plugin",
  "source": "C:\\Users\\...\\gone-plugin",
  "code": "orphan-source-path"
}
code field preserved: YES

=== Phase 3: Snapshot metadata ===
source: derived

=== VERDICT ===
FIX VERIFIED: code field preserved round-trip AND stale detection triggered.
```

Gateway startup after fix (console output):

```
[plugin-registry-snapshot] persisted registry has stale persisted
source (orphan plugin diagnostics detected)
[plugin-registry-snapshot] derived new registry index
```

SQLite `diagnostics_json` contains the `code` field:

```json
[
  {
    "level": "error",
    "message": "plugin path not found: C:\\Users\\...\\gone-plugin",
    "source": "C:\\Users\\...\\gone-plugin",
    "code": "orphan-source-path"
  }
]
```

Without fix 2 (Zod schema missing `code`), the field was silently
stripped by Zod default strip mode during `safeParseWithSchema`.

- **Observed result after fix**: Gateway starts successfully with stale
orphan diagnostics in persisted index. The
`persisted-registry-stale-source` diagnostic is emitted, registry is
re-derived, and orphan diagnostic entries are cleaned up on the next
index write.

- **What was not tested**: Production environment (intentionally avoided).
Cross-platform behavior (macOS/Linux) -- same logic applies but not
explicitly tested on those platforms.

## Changes

- `src/plugins/manifest-types.ts`
- `src/plugins/discovery.ts`
- `src/plugins/plugin-registry-snapshot.ts`
- `src/plugins/plugin-registry-snapshot.test.ts`
- `src/plugins/installed-plugin-index-store.ts`
## Legacy Upgrade Path Verification

Legacy diagnostics from pre-fix versions (no `code` field, no `pluginId`) are also correctly handled by the stale detection logic added in this PR.

### Test Setup

1. Built real SQLite state database with schema from `src/state/openclaw-state-schema.sql`
2. Inserted a legacy "no-code" orphan diagnostic (no `pluginId`, no `code` field)
3. Set up full isolation environment (5 env vars)
4. Ran `loadPluginRegistrySnapshotWithMetadata()` against the legacy state

### Results: ALL CHECKS PASSED ✅

| Check | Description | Result |
|-------|------------|--------|
| 1 | Registry re-derived (stale detected) | ✅ `source: "derived"` |
| 2 | Stale diagnostic emitted | ✅ `persisted-registry-stale-source` |
| 3 | Legacy orphan cleared from in-memory snapshot | ✅ 0 snapshot diagnostics |

### Key Details

- **Legacy diagnostic format**: `{ level: "error", message: "...", source: "..." }` — no `pluginId`, no `code`
- **Detection mechanism**: `hasStalePersistedPluginDiagnostics()` in `plugin-registry-snapshot.ts` has three branches:
  1. `pluginId` + missing source → stale
  2. `code === "orphan-source-path"` → stale  
  3. **Legacy (new)**: no `pluginId` + source missing + `code` undefined → stale
- **Upgrade outcome**: Registry is re-derived from config (clears all legacy diagnostics). A `persisted-registry-stale-source` diagnostic is attached to the result for audit trail.
- **Schema**: `PluginDiagnosticSchema` includes optional `code?: string` field (added in this PR). Legacy diagnostics without the field are still valid under the updated schema.

### Reproducible Test Script

`scripts/verify-legacy-upgrade.cjs` — run from `D:\project\openclaw-dev\`:

```powershell
$env:OPENCLAW_HOME = "D:\project\openclaw-dev\sandbox\home"
$env:OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR = "D:\project\openclaw-dev\sandbox\state"
$env:OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH = "D:\project\openclaw-dev\sandbox\config.json"
$env:OPENCLAW_DISABLE_BUNDLED_PLUGINS = "1"
$env:HOME = "D:\project\openclaw-dev\sandbox"
node scripts/verify-legacy-upgrade.cjs
```

target.title: fix(agents): hard-deadline runtime auth refresh to prevent gateway deadlock
target.body:
## Summary

A long-running gateway can permanently deadlock its entire agent lane on a stuck OAuth auth-refresh. The runtime auth single-flight in `auth-controller.ts` stores the in-flight refresh promise in `runtimeAuthState.refreshInFlight`; every model turn that needs auth does `await runtimeAuthState.refreshInFlight` **with no timeout**. If the underlying provider auth hook (`prepareProviderRuntimeAuth` -> OAuth refresh, keychain read, or cross-agent file-lock wait) never settles, `refreshInFlight` is never cleared and **every subsequent turn hangs forever** awaiting it. The process stays alive and the port stays open, so it looks healthy while no replies are produced.

Observed in production: a gateway froze mid-day right after a token hit expiry. Process alive (11d uptime, port listening) but fully idle since the freeze, zero sockets to the provider, all threads parked, one never-resolving `await`. On-disk token was valid the whole time (a fresh process pre-warmed auth in ~0.7s), and no on-disk lock was held — i.e. a pure in-memory single-flight deadlock.

This adds a hard deadline so the single-flight promise **always** settles:

- New `withRuntimeAuthRefreshDeadline()` + `RUNTIME_AUTH_REFRESH_HARD_TIMEOUT_MS` (300s) in `runtime-auth-refresh.ts`. 300s sits above the OAuth manager's own 120s call timeout plus a peer's 180s stale-lock window, so a legitimately slow cross-agent refresh still completes while a true hang is forced to reject.
- `refreshRuntimeAuth` wraps the refresh operation in that deadline; on timeout it rejects, the `.finally` clears `refreshInFlight`, and all waiters unblock with a descriptive error instead of hanging.
- The `.finally` clear is no longer gated on `generation`: a profile rotation during a slow/hung refresh must still release the handle it owns, otherwise a stale handle wedges the new generation. The existing `refreshInFlight === refreshPromise` identity guard still prevents clobbering a newer refresh.

No behavior change on the happy path (fast refresh resolves long before the deadline). The deadline is a backstop only.

## Repro / Test plan

- [x] `withRuntimeAuthRefreshDeadline` unit tests: rejects after the deadline when work never settles (fake timers), resolves/propagates when work wins the race, passes through unbounded for non-positive timeout, and the default exceeds the OAuth call + stale-lock budget.
- [x] `auth-controller` regression test: a `prepareProviderRuntimeAuth` that hangs forever sets `refreshInFlight`, then after advancing past the hard deadline the wedged handle rejects with `exceeded hard deadline` and is no longer the active in-flight handle.
- [x] Proof the test catches the bug: with the deadline neutralized (timeout `0` = unbounded), the regression test **times out / FAILS**; restored, it passes.
- [x] `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/runtime-auth-refresh.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/auth-controller.test.ts` -> 17 tests pass.
- [x] `pnpm tsgo` clean for touched files; `scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` clean; `pnpm build` clean (no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]`).

Thanks @amittell.


---

## Update: complete the deadlock class (not just the refresh path)

A follow-up audit found the original commit only backstopped ONE of several entry paths into the same auth lock/gate machinery. Both remaining paths could still permanently wedge the agent lane the same way:

1. **Cold-start / profile-rotation path (critical).** `applyApiKeyInfo` (the path `initializeAuthProfile` and `advanceAuthProfile` use, and the first turn a watchdog restart lands on) awaited `resolveApiKeyForCandidate` and `prepareProviderRuntimeAuth` — the exact hook that hung in production — with no deadline. A single shared local `withAuthDeadline` helper now wraps every auth boundary in `auth-controller.ts` (refresh AND cold-start), so a hung provider hook fails the turn over instead of deadlocking the lane.
2. **In-lock keychain / buildApiKey (high).** In `oauth-manager.ts`, `withRefreshCallTimeout` wrapped only the network refresh call; the in-lock keychain store load and `buildApiKey` ran un-deadlined while the cross-agent file lock was held, so a wedged keychain pinned the lock and chain-stalled every same-key refresher via the un-timed `await prev` gate. The whole held-lock critical section is now bounded by `OAUTH_REFRESH_INLOCK_TIMEOUT_MS` (150s), kept strictly between the 120s call timeout and the 180s stale window.

### Added proof
- `auth-controller` cold-start regression test: a `prepareProviderRuntimeAuth` that hangs forever on `initializeAuthProfile` now fails over within the deadline; **neutralizing the backstop makes the test time out / FAIL** (deadlock reproduced), confirming it catches the bug.
- `oauth-manager` invariant test pins `OAUTH_REFRESH_CALL_TIMEOUT_MS < OAUTH_REFRESH_INLOCK_TIMEOUT_MS < stale`.
- All touched suites green (38 tests), tsgo/oxlint/oxfmt clean, `pnpm build` clean.

## Summary

- Fixes the isolated cron pre-execution watchdog treating setup/context phase progress as a stall.
- Keeps the 60s pre-execution guard for the case where the runner starts but emits no phase progress at all.
- Moves setup-like phase progress (`model_resolution`, `auth`, `context_engine`, fallback `runtime_plugins`) under the configured job timeout instead of the hard-coded pre-execution watchdog.
- Out of scope: changing cron config defaults, timeout durations, delivery behavior, or provider/model routing.

Reviewers should focus on whether the watchdog should classify any known phase as progress after runner start, and whether the updated regression expectations match the intended timeout contract.

## Linked context

Closes #93912

Related #93530
Related #93867

Requested by an operator trying to decide whether isolated cron jobs are safe to run again.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- Behavior or issue addressed: isolated cron `agentTurn` jobs can be aborted by the 60s pre-execution watchdog while setup/context phases continue to report progress.
- Real environment tested: local OpenClaw source checkout on Linux arm64 with repository dependencies installed.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cron/service/timer.regression.test.ts`
- Evidence after fix (screenshot, recording, terminal capture, console output, redacted runtime log, linked artifact, or copied live output):

```text
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.cron.config.ts

 RUN  v4.1.8 /tmp/openclaw-fix-clean

      Tests  64 passed (64)
   Start at  03:54:04
   Duration  2.14s (transform 873ms, setup 114ms, import 1.23s, tests 722ms, environment 0ms)

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 5.04s
```

- Observed result after fix: the regression file passes, including coverage that setup/context phase progress stays alive past 60s and only times out on the configured job timeout.
- What was not tested: live scheduled cron against a real provider/channel.
- Proof limitations or environment constraints: this is focused source-level regression proof, not a live production cron run.
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged): before the test expectation update, the old stale test timed out after 120s because it expected the pre-execution watchdog to re-arm on fallback setup progress.

## Tests and validation

Commands run:

- `corepack pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cron/service/timer.regression.test.ts`
- `corepack pnpm exec oxfmt --check --threads=1 src/cron/service/agent-watchdog.ts src/cron/service/timer.regression.test.ts`

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? `No`

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? `No`

Highest-risk area: cron isolated-agent timeout behavior.

target.title: feat(mobile): rename, delete, and create session groups on iOS and Android
target.body:
Closes #101231
Related: #101117

## What Problem This Solves

iOS and Android gained session grouping in #100814, but groups there are write-once: no rename, no delete, and a group only exists while a session carries its category. The web sidebar got full group management in #101117; mobile users were left re-assigning member sessions one by one to reorganize.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both platforms mirror the web semantics. Category section headers gain group actions — a context menu on the iOS Command Center sessions screen ("Rename Group…", "New Group…", "Delete Group…") and a long-press menu on the Android sessions screen. Rename and delete enumerate every member with two `sessions.list` calls (active + archived) using an explicit high limit (the gateway caps an absent `limit` at 100 rows — the same cap the web implementation had to page past), then patch `category` per member best-effort so one failure cannot strand the rest; archived members are included so restores land in the renamed group. Delete keeps sessions and moves them back to Ungrouped. Known custom group names persist client-side (iOS `UserDefaults` key `openclaw:sessions:custom-groups`, matching the web localStorage key; Android SharedPreferences `sessions.customGroups`), so header-created empty groups render as sections and stay usable as move targets. iOS bulk-op enumeration/merge lives in pure `CommandSessionGrouping.members`; Android's lives in `ChatController`, keeping the controller gateway-only.

Non-goals: no group-by on/off toggle on mobile (the mobile screens keep their existing filter/sort controls), and no gateway/protocol changes.

## User Impact

Mobile session groups become maintainable in place: rename a group once instead of per session, delete a group without losing its sessions, and create an empty group before filling it. Group names created or renamed on any platform are the same server-side `category` values, so web and mobile stay consistent.

## Evidence

- Android: `pnpm android:test` (`:app:testPlayDebugUnitTest`) green locally including new tests — known-groups empty-section merge and `ChatController` bulk-op tests asserting per-member patch payloads (archived-only member included), `category:null` on delete, best-effort continuation past a failing patch, and the explicit `limit:10000` enumeration. `pnpm android:lint` (ktlint) green.
- iOS: `pnpm ios:build` green (full app typecheck). Focused simulator tests green for `CommandSessionGroupingTests` (known-groups sections, member merge/dedupe) and `SessionGroupStoreTests` (normalize/rename/remove/UserDefaults round-trip). The unrelated `OpenClawTypographyTests` failure reproduces on current `main` (offenders introduced by #100946/#101198 in `apps/shared` chat files this PR does not touch) and is tracked separately.
- `pnpm native:i18n:check` clean after inventory sync (strings follow the existing plain-literal style of these surfaces).
- Autoreview (Codex, gpt-5.5) on the feature commit: clean — no findings, "patch is correct" (confidence 0.82).

## What Problem This Solves

The core gateway client and the shared gateway-client package maintained parallel option, event, error, validation, and connection-metadata contracts. That duplication made the internal client boundary easy to drift and required core-specific casts and repeated frame guards.

This makes `@openclaw/gateway-client` the canonical client contract owner and moves lightweight inbound frame validation to the published `@openclaw/gateway-protocol/frame-guards` leaf. target.title: fix(qa): restore automatic smoke coverage across channels
target.body:
Related: #101164
Related: #101184
Supersedes: #101187

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where automatic QA Smoke CI selected one shared multi-channel profile, causing the suite resolver to reject the run before any channel scenario could execute.

## Why This Change Was Made

The workflow now plans three deterministic channel-compatible shards from the current smoke profile: one Matrix shard and two execution-cost-balanced Telegram shards. All 89 eligible flow, script, and Playwright scenarios run exactly once. Each shard runs independently while one aggregate required status stays fail-closed. Slack and WhatsApp restart/resume scenarios require their live channel drivers because Crabline does not satisfy those inbound/auth contracts; the silence-sensitive Telegram baseline is isolated from concurrent transport traffic.

## User Impact

target.title: feat(cli): add openclaw promos to discover and claim ClawHub promotional model offers
target.body:
Closes #100234

### What Problem This Solves

ClawHub publishes time-boxed promotional model offers (`GET /api/v1/promotions`), but existing OpenClaw users have no way to activate one short of re-running onboarding or hand-editing config — and no way to *learn about* one without reading an announcement. Offers expire on a schedule, so activation must be fast and must not require an OpenClaw release per promotion.

### Why This Change Was Made

Adds an `openclaw promos` command group (`list`, `claim <slug>`) that turns a claim into a ~30-second flow, plus **passive discovery** riding ClawHub's hosted promotions feed, while treating all remote payloads as strictly declarative:

- Every remote identifier is contract-validated at the parse boundary (`src/infra/clawhub.ts`): slug (`[a-z0-9-]`), model refs (shell-safe, must start with the promotion's declared provider), provider/authChoiceId (identifier grammar), pluginNames (npm package-name grammar, scoped names allowed). Display text is `sanitizeTerminalText`-ed at output. A malformed or compromised promotion cannot make the CLI execute anything, print terminal controls, or emit unsafe copy-paste commands.
- Auth reuses existing machinery end-to-end: unknown auth-choice ids are refused with an "update OpenClaw" message (manifest choices first, install catalog second — mirroring `applyAuthChoiceLoadedPluginProvider`); existing provider credentials are reused only when the provider plugin is actually installed; otherwise the provider's normal auth-choice flow runs (install + enable + auth), with completion revalidated before any config write. `--api-key` follows the shipped `onboard --<provider>-api-key`/`--token` non-interactive contract; provider env vars work with no flag at all.
- Models register through the canonical config mutators (`upsertCanonicalModelConfigEntry`); aliases are held to the `models aliases add` contract and never overwrite existing aliases; plugin enablement is enforced (policy-blocked plugins refuse the claim); setting the suggested default is offered — never forced — and runs the same Codex/Copilot runtime-plugin repair as `openclaw models set`.
- **Passive discovery** (`src/infra/promotions-feed.ts`, `src/commands/models/list.promotions.ts`): a cadence-gated (24h), fail-silent conditional GET of ClawHub's immutable feed snapshot (`GET /api/v1/feeds/promotions`, wire contract `clawhub-promotions` schemaVersion 1, `If-None-Match` → `304`), cached in the shared state DB (two new SQLite tables — no new files) fully separate from `update_check_state` so promo discovery can never delay or break update checks. `models list` then renders an "Available via promotion" group for live offers whose models are not configured (reading only the cache, never the network), tags claimed models `promo` / `promo ended` from claim provenance recorded at claim time, and prints a one-time notice per newly seen offer (suppressed after `promos list`/`claim`, and entirely absent in `--json`/`--plain`). Snapshot sequence is monotonic — a stale edge can never roll the cache back. `promos claim` still always revalidates against the live API, so ClawHub's kill switch wins regardless of feed staleness.
- Zero new config keys, env vars, or state files (state lives in the existing shared SQLite state DB).

### User Impact

Existing users see live offers directly in `openclaw models list` (with a claim command), can run `openclaw promos list` for details, then `openclaw promos claim <slug>` (optionally `--api-key`/`--set-default` for non-interactive use) and immediately use promotional models. Models claimed through a promotion are tagged `promo`, flipping to `promo ended` when the window passes so users learn why a model stopped serving. Nothing about their defaults, aliases, or credentials changes without explicit consent; machine outputs stay clean. Docs: `docs/cli/promos.md` (incl. new passive-discovery section).

### Evidence

- Unit tests: 46 across `src/commands/promos/claim.test.ts` (claim flow incl. provenance recording), `list.test.ts`, `src/infra/clawhub.promotions.test.ts` (payload + feed wire-contract validation, conditional fetch/304), `src/infra/promotions-feed.test.ts` (cache round-trip, cadence gate, `If-None-Match` revalidation, sequence monotonicity, offline fail-silent, notified markers, claim provenance upsert), `src/commands/models/list.promotions.test.ts` (promo/ended tags, section rendering, configured suppression, notice-once, expired-window silence). `pnpm test src/commands/models src/commands/promos src/infra/promotions-feed.test.ts src/infra/clawhub.promotions.test.ts` green (125 + infra).
- Gates: `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`, scoped `scripts/run-oxlint.mjs`, `oxfmt`, `pnpm docs:check-links`, `pnpm docs:map:check`, full `pnpm build` (no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]`; the promotions decorations load through the same lazy-import boundary as the other `models list` modules).
- Live end-to-end against a local ClawHub instance in an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`: first `models list` fetches the real feed (sequence 27), renders the "Available via promotion" group and the 🎁 notice; second run revalidates nothing (cadence gate), keeps the group, suppresses the notice; the state row holds the ETag, sequence, and notified slugs; `models list --json` contains no promotion text. Claim flow live E2E (auth, registration, default) verified previously on the same instance.
- Structured review (Codex/gpt-5.5) run to a clean final pass on each change bundle; earlier passes' findings (auth completeness, terminal sanitization, window trust, slug/model-ref/identifier contracts, scoped plugin names, plugin install/enable enforcement, runtime repair) are each fixed with regression tests. Two reviewer suggestions were consciously rejected with sibling-contract evidence, documented inline: argv `--api-key` (matches shipped onboard non-interactive flags) and provider-credential reuse (deliberate contract; gated by install provenance and plugin policy).

## Summary

Adds a 24h timeline strip to the Cron Jobs page in the Control UI, providing an at-a-glance view of today's scheduled tasks.

Closes #40644

## Screenshots

### Dark Theme — Full View
![Full page dark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xvchris/cron-calendar-screenshots/main/dark-full.jpg)
*Summary strip with always-on chip, 24h timeline with NOW indicator, cluster badges, color-coded dots*

### Cluster Hover — Overlapping Jobs
![Cluster hover](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xvchris/cron-calendar-screenshots/main/cluster-hover.jpg)
*Hovering the ④ cluster at 22:00 shows 4 overlapping jobs with color-coded dots and times*

### Single Dot Hover — Job Info Popup
![Dot hover](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xvchris/cron-calendar-screenshots/main/dot-hover.jpg)
*Hovering oss-scan dot shows schedule, status, duration, and "Click → view run history" hint*

### Light Theme
![Light theme](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xvchris/cron-calendar-screenshots/main/light-theme.jpg)
*Full light theme support via existing CSS variables*

## Features

### Timeline Strip
- **24-hour timeline track** with grid lines and time labels
- **NOW indicator** — red vertical line showing current time, auto-updates every 60s
- **Color-coded dots** — each job gets a distinct color; green for past (ok), blue pulse for future (pending)
- **Cluster badges** — nearby dots (within 2.5%) auto-merge into a numbered badge; hover to see the full list
- **Hover popups** — JS-driven mouseenter/mouseleave with 150ms debounce for reliable hover behavior
- **Click navigation** — past dots jump to Run History (filtered), future dots scroll to job details
- **Zoom controls** — 24h (full day), Work (08:00–20:00), Now±3h (centered on current time)

### Always-On Chips
- High-frequency jobs (every <10min or cron `*/N` where N≤10) are displayed as chips in the summary strip instead of cluttering the timeline
- Hover to see: View Details / View History / Run Now actions
- Click to jump to run history

### Other
- **Mobile fallback** — timeline hidden on narrow screens, replaced by a simple text list of upcoming jobs
- **Full i18n** — all strings use `t()`, translations added for en, zh-CN, zh-TW, de, es, pt-BR
- **Theme support** — uses only existing CSS variables, works in both dark and light modes
- **No existing features removed** — purely additive changes to the view layer

## Files Changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `ui/src/ui/helpers/cron-timeline.ts` | **New** — Timeline computation (zoom, clustering, high-freq detection) |
| `ui/src/ui/views/cron.ts` | Added timeline rendering between summary and workspace |
| `ui/src/styles/components.css` | Added timeline CSS (523 lines) |
| `ui/src/i18n/locales/*.ts` | Added `cron.timeline.*` keys to all 6 locales |

## Testing

- Computed timeline data from existing `CronProps` — no controller changes needed
- All new code is additive; existing view functions untouched
- TypeScript strict mode compatible

target.title: fix(update): keep self-updates on the running install's global root
target.body:
## Summary

- `resolveGlobalInstallTarget` now prefers the global root that the resolved package root lives in for npm targets
- the `npm root -g` probe only decides the target when no package root is known
- a probe result under an ephemeral per-Node prefix (Homebrew Cellar, nvm/n/asdf/volta version dirs) is never adopted, reusing the classifier #93650 added for npm command selection

## The bug

Package self-updates picked their install target from `npm root -g` even when the package root the process is running from was already known. If PATH's npm doesn't belong to the running install's Node tree, the probe points at a different global root. The update installs there, reports success, and the install that's actually running stays on the old version. Probably the same failure shape as #98618.

Concrete case from my gateway's update handoff log (2026.5.28 updating to 2026.6.11): the launchd service PATH had Homebrew's bin first and nvm's second, so the managed `openclaw update --yes` ran nvm's npm shim under Homebrew's node. nvm's npm has no builtin prefix config, so it derived its default prefix from the realpathed execPath:

```
"root": "/opt/homebrew/Cellar/node/26.3.1/lib/node_modules/openclaw",
"before": { "version": null },
"global update": ".../.nvm/versions/node/v24.10.0/bin/npm i -g
    --prefix /opt/homebrew/Cellar/node/26.3.1/lib/node_modules/.openclaw-update-stage-2EAbUE openclaw@latest"
```

`"before": null` means the update created a brand-new tree inside the versioned Cellar directory (which the next `brew upgrade node` deletes) and ran doctor from it, while the running nvm install kept serving 2026.5.28. Doctor then flagged an entrypoint mismatch and re-staged the service plist, compounding the skew.

#93650 already stops the per-Node npm *command* from being used, but the probed *target root* was never validated, and `honorPackageRoot` is only set on managed-service redirects, so the "roots match, but the service environment's npm points elsewhere" case fell through.

## Fix

In `resolveGlobalInstallTarget`, for npm targets:

1. if the package root is known, its own `node_modules` parent is the target (this is where the running install lives, so it's the only tree worth updating)
2. the `npm root -g` probe is a fallback for when no package root is known
3. a probe result whose prefix is an ephemeral per-Node path is rejected outright

When the probe agrees with the running root (the normal case) nothing changes. pnpm and bun targets are untouched. No existing test needed modification.

## Verification

- `pnpm check` passes
- `pnpm build` passes
- `pnpm vitest run src/infra/update-global.test.ts src/infra/update-runner.test.ts src/cli/update-cli.test.ts` — 272 passed (3 new tests: Cellar probe rejected in favor of the running root, matching probe still adopted, probe failure falls back to the running root)
- full `pnpm test`: 723/724, the one failure (`extensions/litellm/index.test.ts`) reproduces identically on a clean `origin/main` worktree, so it's pre-existing and unrelated


## Real behavior proof

Live run on the machine from the incident log, using the PR build packed with `pnpm pack` (plus `@openclaw/ai` packed from the same commit and vendored via an npm override, since it isn't published). The artifact was installed with real npm into an nvm-style tree, its version field set back to `2026.6.9`, and `update --yes` executed under a PATH whose npm derives an ephemeral Homebrew Cellar prefix — the same skew as the incident:

```
$ npm root -g        # under the skewed PATH
/tmp/ocproof4/opt/homebrew/Cellar/node/26.3.1/lib/node_modules

$ node .../v24.10.0/lib/node_modules/openclaw/dist/index.js update --dry-run
  Root: /private/tmp/ocproof4/home/.nvm/versions/node/v24.10.0/lib/node_modules/openclaw
  Mode: npm
  Current version: 2026.6.9
  Target version: 2026.6.11

$ node .../v24.10.0/lib/node_modules/openclaw/dist/index.js update --yes
  ✓ global install swap (561ms)
  ✓ openclaw doctor (4.69s)
Total time: 13.48s

after: package.json in the running tree = 2026.6.11
Cellar root contents: (empty — nothing diverted)
```

The running install's version actually changed in place, and the ephemeral Cellar root the probe pointed at stayed empty. On stock 2026.5.28 the same skew installed a full copy into `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/node/26.3.1/lib/node_modules/openclaw` (`"before": { "version": null }` in the pre-fix handoff log quoted above) while the running install stayed stale. (A trailing `uv_cwd` ENOENT after the success line is the demo shell's cwd being swapped out from under it by the install swap, not an updater failure.)

## Review follow-up

target.title: fix(markdown-core): CJK-friendly emphasis flanking so **标签：**正文 renders bold (#101120)
target.body:
Fixes #101120

## What Problem This Solves

Bold written as `**标题：**内容` (full-width CJK punctuation immediately inside the closing `**`, no following space) renders as literal `**` on Telegram and every channel using the shared markdown renderer. CommonMark's flanking rules require a closing delimiter preceded by punctuation to be followed by whitespace/punctuation — but CJK text has no inter-word spaces, so the extremely common `**label：**text` idiom from CJK LLM output never qualifies.

## Fix

Small local amendment in `packages/markdown-core/src/ir.ts`: wraps markdown-it's inline delimiter scanning so East Asian characters adjacent to a delimiter count as letters for flanking (per the CJK-friendly flanking amendment semantics from markdown-it-cjk-friendly, implemented locally — **no new dependency**).

- Only activates when a CJK code point is adjacent to the delimiter run; ASCII/Latin behavior is unchanged CommonMark
- Whitespace-adjacent handling unchanged; `_` emphasis unchanged; code spans/links unaffected
- Fixes all channels through the shared renderer, not just Telegram

## Evidence

- Repro test in `extensions/telegram/src/format.test.ts` (fails without the fix): `边界：**社区显示：**Fable 与 **有效**。` now renders both bold spans
- New `packages/markdown-core/src/ir.emphasis-cjk.test.ts`: Chinese/Japanese/Korean cases plus regressions (ASCII `**bold** text`, intraword `foo**bar**baz`, code spans, links)
- Focused run: 2 files, 73 tests, all pass

target.title: feat(agents): per-agent outbound A2A allowlist override
target.body:
## Summary

- Add `agents.list[].tools.agentToAgent.allow` to control which agents a specific agent may contact via session tools (`sessions_send`, `sessions_list`, `sessions_history`, `session_status`)
- When unset, the agent falls back to the global `tools.agentToAgent.allow` list; when set to explicit IDs, only those targets are reachable; `[]` isolates the agent from all cross-agent access
- The global `tools.agentToAgent.allow` continues to act as a participation gate (both requester and target must match it) before per-agent outbound rules are evaluated
- Outbound-only semantics: only the requester's override is checked, not the target's
- Replace `matchesAllow` with `matchesGlobalParticipation` and add `evaluateAccess()` returning a structured `AgentToAgentDenyReason` so all call sites produce context-aware error messages via `formatAgentToAgentAccessError()`
- Scrub deleted agent references from per-agent outbound allowlists in `pruneAgentConfig()`

### Example config (hub-spoke pattern)

```json
{
  "tools": {
    "agentToAgent": { "enabled": true, "allow": ["*"] }
  },
  "agents": {
    "list": [
      { "id": "david",  "tools": { "agentToAgent": { "allow": ["*"] } } },
      { "id": "spoke",  "tools": { "agentToAgent": { "allow": ["david"] } } },
      { "id": "kelly",  "tools": { "agentToAgent": { "allow": ["david"] } } }
    ]
  }
}
```

spoke→david ✅ | spoke→kelly ❌ | david→anyone ✅

## Test plan

- [x] `sessions-access.test.ts`: per-agent override, deny-all `[]`, global gate, target override ignored (outbound-only), fallback to global when unset
- [x] `sessions.test.ts`: per-agent outbound deny during label lookup in `sessions_send`
- [x] `openclaw-tools.session-status.test.ts`: per-agent outbound deny for cross-agent `session_status`
- [x] `agents.test.ts`: `pruneAgentConfig` scrubs deleted agent from per-agent allowlists
- [x] Build passes
- [x] Manual: configure hub-spoke agents (david/spoke/kelly), verify per-agent outbound rules — see `Real behavior proof` section below

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: per-agent outbound `agentToAgent.allow` correctly gates cross-agent session tool access. Hub-spoke topology used: `david` (hub, `allow=["*"]`), `spoke` (allow=`["david"]`), `kelly` (allow=`["david"]`). Validates the new `evaluateAccess()` decision pipeline reaches the documented per-agent outbound semantics, with the structured `per_agent_outbound` deny reason surfaced via `formatAgentToAgentAccessError()`.

- **Real environment tested**: Ubuntu 22.04 (kernel 5.15), Node 22.22.0, pnpm 10. Branch HEAD `55819f6f43` of `repair/pr-39102-a2a-refresh` (this PR rebased on current main). Live invocation of the production export `createAgentToAgentPolicy` from `src/plugin-sdk/session-visibility.ts` — no mocks, no test runner, the same code path that backs `sessions_send`, `sessions_list`, `sessions_history`, and `session_status` at runtime.

- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

  1. Author a hub-spoke `OpenClawConfig` matching the docs example (david hub + spoke + kelly).
  2. Build `policy = createAgentToAgentPolicy(cfg)`.
  3. Call `policy.evaluateAccess(requester, target)` for the five edge pairs.
  4. Run with: `pnpm tsx proof-hub-spoke.ts` (the script imports the worktree source directly so the running code is the patched export).

- **Evidence after fix**: terminal output, copied verbatim from `node` stdout via `tsx`.

  ```
  # per-agent A2A allowlist — hub-spoke proof
  # config: david=hub (allow *), spoke=spoke (allow david), kelly=spoke (allow david)

  [ok ] spoke -> david: ALLOWED
  [ok ] spoke -> kelly: DENIED (reason=per_agent_outbound)
  [ok ] david -> kelly: ALLOWED
  [ok ] david -> spoke: ALLOWED
  [ok ] kelly -> spoke: DENIED (reason=per_agent_outbound)

  all cases match expected behavior
  ```

- **Observed result after fix**: all five real invocations matched the documented hub-spoke semantics. Cross-spoke calls (`spoke -> kelly`, `kelly -> spoke`) were denied with the structured `per_agent_outbound` reason code from `AgentToAgentDecision`. Hub-rooted calls (`david -> spoke`, `david -> kelly`) and spoke-to-hub (`spoke -> david`) were allowed. Process exit code: `0`. Console output above is the literal stdout, no post-processing.

- **What was not tested**: end-to-end IPC roundtrip through the live `sessions_send` agent process pair (single-machine ACP transport). The four session call sites all delegate the access decision to the single `evaluateAccess()` policy proven above, and the wiring of each call site is covered by the unit tests already listed in the Test plan.

target.title: fix(infra): swallow mid-stream read errors in session-cost readJsonlRecords
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readJsonlRecords` reads session transcript JSONL through a `readline` interface backed by `fs.createReadStream`. A mid-stream read failure can reject diagnostic session-log reads. Swallowing that failure in the shared reader is unsafe, though, because the same reader feeds the durable usage cache and could persist a partial scan as a fresh complete entry.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the shared JSONL reader strict so cache scans fail before replacing the durable entry. Add a best-effort wrapper only for `loadSessionLogs`, where returning the records read before a stream failure is appropriate diagnostic behavior.

The regression coverage also verifies that a failed append-only cache refresh rejects, leaves the previous cache bytes unchanged, and reports the changed transcript as pending instead of fresh.

## User Impact

Session-log diagnostics no longer surface raw mid-stream read errors, while incomplete usage scans cannot silently poison the durable usage cache.

## Evidence

- `OPENCLAW_LOCAL_CHECK_MODE=throttled node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/session-cost-usage.stream-errors.test.ts src/infra/session-cost-usage.test.ts` — 67 tests passed.
